passages.t: ‘As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master’
passages.happening:
Psalm 123 is one of the shortest Songs of Ascents. It begins, “A song of ascents. I lift up my eyes to You, the One enthroned in heaven” (verse 1).

Then a picture from a household. “As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes are on the LORD our God until He shows us mercy” (verse 2).

The prayer is simple. “Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much contempt” (verse 3). “We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
In Psalm 121 the pilgrim lifted his eyes to the hills. Here the eyes go higher still, to God on his throne. The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents.

In a large household, servants watched the hand of the master or mistress. A small movement could call them, send them off, or hand them bread or wages. Watching the hand meant being ready, and depending on it. The psalm includes both a man and a woman: a servant with his master, a maidservant with the woman who ran the house.

The people here are not facing an army. They are being mocked. ‘The arrogant’ means those who are comfortable and secure, and ‘the proud’ those who look down from a height. Many scholars think of the small community back from exile, mocked by its neighbours. Nehemiah prayed in the same words: “Hear us, O God, for we are despised” (Nehemiah 4:4). The psalm names no one, so it has been prayed by many people in many places.
passages.later:
In the Gospels, people who were looked down on cried out the same word: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47). A tax collector stood far off and prayed, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

Peter wrote to believers who were insulted for their faith: “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed” (1 Peter 4:14).
passages.asks:
Have you been on the receiving end of contempt, the look that says you do not matter? Psalm 123 does not ask you to pretend it does not hurt. It says ‘much’ twice. It turns your eyes from the faces of the scornful to the hand of God.

And notice the word ‘until’. The servants keep watching until mercy comes. That is what waiting on God looks like.
